introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One hour): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 12 below shows a simple diagram of a p - n junction.

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_10_fig_1.png)

(i) Name the section labelled Q and explain why it is called that way.

(ii) How can the terminals of the battery be connected in figure 12 to produce a forward bias?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Section Q is the depletion layer (depletion region).** Electrons diffuse from the n-type side across the junction into the p-type side, where they recombine with holes; holes diffuse the other way and recombine with electrons. This leaves a thin region on each side of the junction that has been **depleted of free (mobile) charge carriers**. Only the fixed, ionised impurity atoms remain (positive donor ions on the n side, negative acceptor ions on the p side), so the layer is called the depletion layer; it behaves as an insulator and sets up a potential barrier across the junction.

**(ii) Forward bias.** Connect the **positive terminal** of the battery to terminal **X** (the p-type side) and the **negative terminal** to terminal **Y** (the n-type side), with a resistor in series to limit the current. The applied p.d. opposes the barrier potential, the depletion layer becomes narrower, and a current flows once the applied voltage exceeds about $0.6\ \mathrm{V}$ for silicon.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The family of curves in figure 13 shows the output characteristics of a transistor.

![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_10_fig_2.png)

(i) Comment on the dependence of $I_C$ on $V_{CE}$.

(ii) Construct a table of values that can be used to determine the transfer characteristics of the above transistor at a constant $V_{CE}$ of $7.5\ \mathrm{V}$.

(iii) Use the table in b(ii) above to draw a graph and from it, determine the d.c. transfer ratio of the transistor.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Dependence of $I_C$ on $V_{CE}$.** For each value of the base current $I_B$:

- for $V_{CE}$ below about $2\ \mathrm{V}$, $I_C$ **rises steeply** with $V_{CE}$ (the saturation region);
- above about $2\ \mathrm{V}$ the curve is **almost horizontal**: $I_C$ hardly depends on $V_{CE}$ (it rises only very slightly). Beyond the knee, $I_C$ is controlled almost entirely by the base current $I_B$, not by $V_{CE}$, and a larger $I_B$ gives a larger, equally flat, $I_C$.

**(ii) Table at $V_{CE} = 7.5\ \mathrm{V}$** (read up from $7.5\ \mathrm{V}$ on the horizontal axis to each curve, then across to the $I_C$ axis):

| $I_B$ / $\mu\mathrm{A}$ | 25 | 50 | 75 | 100 | 125 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $I_C$ / mA | 2.0 | 3.9 | 5.9 | 7.9 | 9.9 |

**(iii) Graph and d.c. transfer ratio.** Plot $I_C$ (vertical, in mA) against $I_B$ (horizontal, in $\mu\mathrm{A}$), choosing scales that fill the paper. The five points lie on a **straight line through (almost) the origin**: $I_C$ is proportional to $I_B$. Gradient of the line (taking the end points):
$$\frac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B} = \frac{(9.9 - 2.0)\times10^{-3}}{(125 - 25)\times10^{-6}} = 79.$$
Because the line passes through the origin, the d.c. transfer ratio (d.c. current gain) is
$$h_{FE} = \frac{I_C}{I_B} = \frac{7.9\times10^{-3}}{100\times10^{-6}} = 79\quad(\text{each point gives } 78 \text{ to } 80).$$
**The d.c. transfer ratio is about $79$ (it has no unit).**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What is a p-n junction?

(ii) Explain how a depletion layer is formed in the p-n junction.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A p-n junction is the boundary (interface) between a p-type and an n-type region formed in a **single crystal** of semiconductor, by doping one part of the crystal with acceptor atoms (p-type, majority carriers: holes) and the other with donor atoms (n-type, majority carriers: electrons).

**(ii)** When the two regions are formed, there are many electrons in the n side and many holes in the p side, so the free electrons **diffuse** across the junction into the p side and the holes diffuse into the n side. Near the junction they meet and recombine. This leaves, on the n side, positive donor ions that are fixed in the lattice, and on the p side negative acceptor ions: a region with no free carriers (the depletion layer) and an electric field across it. The field (a p.d. of about $0.6\ \mathrm{V}$ in silicon) opposes further diffusion, and the layer stops growing when the diffusion of carriers and the drift due to the field balance.
